Projectile explodes near tanker 50 nautical miles off Dubai as Gulf shipping attacks mount
body: Incidents without damage rarely move oil much on their own, but where this one happened matters for pricing. An attack near the UAE coast, inside the Gulf, puts loading routes that had looked relatively safe back in the risk picture, which tends to show up first in war-risk insurance premiums and tanker freight rates rather than in headline crude prices. Asian refiners, the biggest buyers of Gulf crude, are the most exposed to any further disruption. With US markets shut for Thanksgiving and liquidity thin, a more serious incident could cause an exaggerated price move before the full market returns.
No one was hurt and nothing was damaged, but a blast near a tanker off Dubai shows that the threat to Gulf oil shipping is no longer confined to the Strait of Hormuz.

A tanker reported an explosion from an unknown projectile close to the vessel about 50 nautical miles west of Dubai late on Wednesday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said. It's the latest in a run of attacks on shipping that has kept Gulf oil supply under pressure.

The incident happened at 2130 GMT on November 25 (1630 US Eastern). The ship's master reported that the crew were safe and accounted for, with no damage to the tanker and no environmental impact. UKMTO, which monitors commercial shipping in the region, advised vessels to transit with caution while authorities investigate. It didn't identify the tanker or say who fired the projectile.

The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and Oman, normally carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil. Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, Tehran has tried to close the strait, and the United States has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports. The International Maritime Organization has confirmed more than 130 incidents involving commercial vessels in the Gulf, the strait and the Gulf of Oman since the war began.

November has been especially busy. Reported attacks in and around the strait have reached their highest level since the conflict began, according to maritime data cited by CNN, as Tehran tries to reassert control while oil prices fall. This week, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers hit naval mines and caught fire in the strait despite a US escort, and Iran's navy said another tanker struck a mine east of the strait on Wednesday. On Sunday, UKMTO reported a tanker involved in an incident with military forces in the Gulf of Oman.

Wednesday's incident stands out for its location. It took place inside the Gulf, well west of the strait and close to the UAE coast, echoing earlier November attacks on tankers off Qatar and Saudi Arabia. That suggests the risk is spread across Gulf shipping lanes rather than confined to the chokepoint itself.

Oil is still moving, but at reduced levels. Shipping data from Kpler put oil flows through Hormuz at about half of pre-war levels as of November 24, and shipments through the strait fell in the first half of November as attacks increased. US-escorted transits have helped keep some traffic moving. Iran has also reportedly allowed vessels linked to Iraq, Qatar, China and India to pass, which suggests it is managing who uses the strait rather than shutting it completely.

That partial recovery explains why prices have eased in recent weeks despite the violence. Brent crude was trading around $91 a barrel late on Wednesday, up more than 2% on the day, but still well below its wartime peak.

The risk for the oil market is that each new incident, especially further inside the Gulf, raises insurance and freight costs and could deter shipowners who have only recently returned. For now, the market appears to be treating attacks that cause no damage as background noise. A strike that disables a tanker or hits loading infrastructure near the UAE or Saudi coast would be a different matter, and would likely bring back the supply premium quickly.

news.title: Gold claws back $160 from a 14-month low, but one candle doesn't necessarily make a bottom
body: Reclaiming $3,500 gives gold bulls a floor to defend, but there's little sign of a confirmed turn until prices clear last week's high near $3,900. Silver followed the same path, bouncing from below $38 to above $41, which suggests broad short covering across precious metals rather than buying driven by gold alone. With US markets closed for Thanksgiving and Friday a short session, thin liquidity could exaggerate the next move in either direction. The bigger test comes with the Fed's December 9 decision, when the bank's guidance on further hikes is likely to matter more for real yields, and for gold, than the hike itself.
Gold found buyers at its lowest level since September 2025, but bank forecasts ranging from $3,340 to $5,000 show how little agreement there is on where this correction ends.

Gold made a sharp turnaround on Wednesday, recovering about $160 from a 14-month low to close near the top of its range. It did so even as US data gave the Federal Reserve more reason to keep raising rates.

The metal fell to around $3,425 an ounce after the October PCE report, its weakest level since September 2025. That broke the $3,500 support that had held through last week's rout. Core PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred gauge, rose to 3.3% from 3.1%, and third-quarter GDP growth came in at 4.3%, well ahead of expectations. Buyers then stepped in, and gold finished near $3,590, up almost 1% on the day.

The rebound came from the bond and currency markets rather than from any rush to safety. Treasury yields fell after the data and the dollar slipped, while pricing for a December Fed hike eased slightly from near-certain levels. Wall Street also recovered, with the Dow erasing a deep intraday loss to close higher. That eased the margin-driven selling that had forced some investors to sell gold to raise cash during last week's slide of roughly 9%.

Whether Wednesday marks a bottom is another matter. Natixis precious metals analyst Bernard Dahdah expects gold could fall to $3,340 by January. His stress test assumes central bank buying drops a quarter below 2025 levels, and he sees signs that the official-sector demand behind the rally is fading. He points to Poland, whose central bank has reached its 700-tonne reserve target, and argues that most of the accumulation is likely done. Higher rates, a stronger dollar and softer investment demand complete his bearish case.

Other banks see the selloff as a reset rather than the end of the bull market. UBS forecasts gold at $5,000 by the end of 2027 and still rates the metal Attractive, citing central bank diversification, rising sovereign debt and Chinese demand. Goldman Sachs expects $4,650 over the same period, JPMorgan $4,500 and Commerzbank $4,100.

Even after Wednesday's bounce, gold is still roughly a third below its January record close above $5,400. The Fed decides on December 9, and a hike that month is still close to fully priced. One strong candle may be the start of a base, but it doesn't necessarily make a bottom.

news.title: Gold bulls may have been waiting months for a chart like this
body: The daily gold futures chart shows an interesting convergence of three technical references, following a substantial decline from the record high of $5,626.80.

The zoomed-out chart: Gold has been trading within a broad ascending channel spanning several years. Since reaching its record high in early 2026, however, gold has developed a descending channel within that much larger bullish structure.
The latest selloff has brought gold to the lower boundaries of both channels, creating an area of potential technical support.

The zoomed-in chart: Gold futures briefly broke below both channel boundaries and the horizontal price reference at $3,433.18, reaching a low of $3,425.20 before recovering to $3,571.70 at the time of the chart snapshot.
That represents a rebound of approximately 4.28% from the session low, leaving a prominent lower wick on the developing daily candle.
Long-term support: The lower boundary of a multiyear ascending channel is being tested, putting the broader bullish structure under scrutiny.
Potential downside exhaustion: Gold has also tested and recovered above the lower boundary of its 2026 descending channel.
Possible failed breakdown: The recovery above $3,433.18 and both trendlines suggests that sellers have, so far, struggled to sustain prices below these technical references.
The convergence of these three elements is more interesting than a test of an isolated trendline or horizontal support level.
The developing daily candle is encouraging for gold bulls, but its closing price and the market's behavior over the next few sessions could be more revealing.

Sustained trading above both channel boundaries would strengthen the case for a meaningful recovery. Conversely, renewed selling and sustained acceptance below $3,425.20 would weaken that interpretation and raise concerns about the integrity of the multiyear ascending channel.

For longer-term gold investors, this is an area worth monitoring for potential accumulation opportunities. For active traders, the immediate question is whether the sharp rejection of lower prices develops into a more sustainable reversal.
Gold does not need to end its 2026 downtrend for a substantial recovery to take place. Even a rebound within the descending channel could present opportunities.
The chart offers a compelling location to investigate a potential bottom, not confirmation that one has already been established.

news.title: US treasury sells $44 billion of 7-year notes at a high yield of 4.708%
body: The auction was mixed but still better than average. The high yield came in 1.0 basis point above the when-issued level, and the bid to cover was a touch below average. Indirect bidders took a smaller share than usual, but stronger direct demand more than made up for that shortfall, leaving dealers with just 8.61% of the issue. The lighter dealer takedown was a positive that tipped the grade to above average but still on the border between a C+ and a B-.
